Kutaisi New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kutaisi, Georgia

Not demolished. Kutaisi, capital of the medieval United Kingdom of Georgia and later the Imeretian Kingdom, has recorded Jewish presence since the mid-17th century; 19th-century French travelers noted Jews made up roughly half the city's population, concentrated in petty trade within a dense central quarter. Two stone synagogues stood by the early 19th century, with a third built in 1886 (or 1888, per differing sources). Jewish population peaked at 8,864 (84% of the city) in 1897, settling around 5,000 by the early 20th century. This cemetery, also called Sapichkhia, was established in the second half of the 19th century as a shared multi-faith burial ground for Georgian Orthodox, Armenian, and Jewish sections, each separately defined, within what was then dense pine forest. Its oldest legible Jewish tombstone dates to 1892; a newspaper reported 26 stolen tombstones as early as 1878. The cemetery remains active today, with its most recent burial in 2020.
